source: World Religions II — lecture and readings, 2026-09-24

cards.front: Which region does World Religions II focus on?
cards.back: East Asia — the “global East”

cards.front: Which countries does the “global East” cover in this course?
cards.back: China, Japan, North and South Korea, and a little Vietnam

cards.front: Besides the countries themselves, who else is included in the course's scope?
cards.back: Diaspora communities

cards.front: How is the word “cult” used in this class?
cards.back: As a neutral term for a small religious group

cards.front: What does the neutral use of “cult” not rule out discussing?
cards.back: Religions considered dangerous, marginalised, or exploitative

cards.text: The instructor's criteria for religion (1–4): {{c1::a god, gods, or God}}; {{c2::a place of worship}}; {{c3::a holy book or scripture}}; {{c4::a leader, leaders, or specialists}}
The instructor's criteria for religion (5–8): {{c1::a founder}}; {{c2::actions}}; {{c3::belief}}; {{c4::faith}}
The instructor's criteria for religion (9–11): {{c1::vows}}; {{c2::exclusivity}}; {{c3::institutional acceptance — do other people think it is a religion?}}

cards.front: What does “institutional acceptance” mean as a criterion for religion?
cards.back: Whether other people regard it as a religion

cards.front: What did the class discussion offer as features of religion?
cards.back: Transmission, a theology or worldview, ritual devotional practice, sacred space, a historical figure, doctrine, faith, a higher power, and community

cards.front: How does the status of Siddhartha Gautama complicate a god-centred definition of religion?
cards.back: He is always a person who performs miracles, but not always a god

cards.front: How do East Asian traditions treat the line between supernatural and natural?
cards.back: As a continuum, rather than the clear line drawn in western religions

cards.front: Which two traditions are named as not focusing on the worship of a deity?
cards.back: Daoism and Confucianism

cards.front: What do some forms of Buddhism not require?
cards.back: Prayer or attendance at a temple — and some follow no sacred text

cards.front: Exclusivity is one of the instructor's criteria for religion — how do most East Asian religions stand on it?
cards.back: They fail it — most are inclusive rather than exclusive

cards.front: Which East Asian practice looks contradictory from a western definition of religion?
cards.back: Temples and praying directed at someone who is not a god

cards.front: What does the lecture say about people's views of a religion, including their own?
cards.back: They are often subjective

cards.front: What is said to be mutable about a religion?
cards.back: Which aspects are considered most important

cards.front: On what does the perceived importance of a religion's aspects depend?
cards.back: Place, time, and sect

cards.front: Which two countries in the region are officially atheist?
cards.back: China and North Korea

cards.front: What is the status of religion in North Korea officially?
cards.back: All religions are banned

cards.front: How many religions are permitted in China, and which?
cards.back: Five — Buddhism, Taoism, Islam, Protestantism, and Catholicism

cards.front: Despite official atheism, what is true in both China and North Korea?
cards.back: Things we could call religion are still practised

cards.text: Why praying or visiting a shrine may not count as religious practice: {{c1::practice and faith are only loosely associated}}; {{c2::some take a “try anything” approach}}; {{c3::religion can be a vessel for values or tradition rather than belief}}

cards.front: What stance does the course take on defining religion?
cards.back: To be flexible about what a religion is and how it is practised

cards.front: Which distinction does the lecture say to keep in mind throughout?
cards.back: Between doctrine or doxa — the texts — and how religion is practised or perceived

cards.text: The definitional problem runs both ways: {{c1::some things we would call a religion, its people do not}}; and {{c2::things we would not call religious, others do}}

cards.front: What kind of concept is the “Global East”, on the reading's account?
cards.back: A cultural and social one

cards.front: What does the Global East comprise?
cards.back: East Asian societies and ethnic communities, together with the diaspora

cards.front: Why does the reading argue the term “Global East” is needed?
cards.back: A Euro- or North-Atlantic-centric viewpoint cannot properly understand these communities

cards.front: When was the East/West division of the world most used, and why?
cards.back: During the Cold War, with its political and ideological battles

cards.front: Which division of the world became more popular from the 1970s, and what is it chiefly about?
cards.back: North versus South — chiefly developed versus others

cards.text: The reading's argument: the Global East fits {{c1::neither East/West nor North/South}}, because ideologically {{c2::some sided with the west and some with the east}} and economically {{c3::some count as global south despite lying in the northern hemisphere}}

cards.front: In which three Asian countries has communism persisted?
cards.back: China, North Korea, and Vietnam

cards.front: How does the reading say the persistence of communism should be treated?
cards.back: As having a large social impact that must be understood, not brushed off

cards.front: Which was the first developed country in East Asia, and which is named as currently surging?
cards.back: Japan was first; Vietnam is experiencing an economic upsurge

cards.front: What counter-example does the reading give to the global-north category?
cards.back: Some eastern European countries that were supposed to be global north are now struggling

cards.front: Who first argued for a link between religion and economy, and what link?
cards.back: Max Weber — between Protestantism and modern capitalism

cards.front: What is the reading's verdict on Max Weber?
cards.back: That many of his ideas are valuable but a lot of his main conceptualisations miss the mark

cards.front: What population comparison does the reading use against Euro-centric models?
cards.back: The western powers total about 1.1 billion, against about 2.3 billion in East and Southeast Asia — roughly 30% of the world the model fails to account for

cards.front: What does the reading say western scholars over-focus on regarding Christianity?
cards.back: Its movement into the “global south”

cards.front: What do western scholars, Weber among them, get wrong about Confucianism?
cards.back: They treat it as far more prevalent than surveys show — very few in East Asia or the diaspora self-identify as Confucian

cards.front: Why might someone identify as Buddhist or Confucian yet deny being religious?
cards.back: Because they do not consider those traditions to be religions

cards.front: What kind of problem does the reading say underlies this?
cards.back: A language problem — meanings were altered when the terms were translated and imported

cards.front: What does the reading say about the word “religion” in everyday East Asian language?
cards.back: For many, it is still not an everyday concept

cards.front: How does the reading characterise political leadership on what counts as religion?
cards.back: As “confused and confusing”

cards.front: In China, how are Confucianism and Daoism officially classified?
cards.back: Confucianism is not a religion; Daoism is

cards.front: How does the reading describe modern atheism as a confounding factor?
cards.back: As a secularist ideology — a modern phenomenon

cards.front: What does the reading claim about atheism rates in East Asia?
cards.back: By some measures, East Asian societies have the highest proportions of people claiming to be atheists

cards.meaning: Robert Bellah's 1985 concept for Americans who mix and choose their own religion

cards.front: Who introduced Sheilaism, where, and when?
cards.back: Robert Bellah, in America, in 1985

cards.front: Why is Sheilaism relevant to the Global East?
cards.back: The reading argues it can be applied to East Asia in some senses

cards.front: Which related phenomena does the reading say also appear in East Asia?
cards.back: New Age spiritualism, being “spiritual but not religious”, and religious “nones”

cards.front: What was the course of secularization in China?
cards.back: A state-engineered programme — but religiousness has been rising since the 1970s

cards.front: Does the Chinese pattern of secularization hold across the region?
cards.back: No — not all countries follow it

cards.front: What did the first westerners to study Korea observe?
cards.back: That Koreans called on supernatural powers for supernatural reasons

cards.front: Which three traditions have been prominent in Korea since early history?
cards.back: Buddhism, Confucianism, and Shamanism

cards.front: What effect has modernization had on demand for religion in Korea?
cards.back: None — it has not affected it

cards.front: What proportion of Koreans have a religious affiliation, and what is true of the rest?
cards.back: About 50% — and many of those claiming not to be religious still engaged in religious activities

cards.front: How does the reading describe the Korean approach to religion?
cards.back: Instrumentalist — like choosing the best tool for a given job

cards.front: What is the gap between Korean religious groups and Korean practice?
cards.back: Groups sometimes claim exclusivity, but people do not always practise it that way

cards.front: How was Buddhism received when it arrived in Korea?
cards.back: It caused a stir, but was eventually accepted

cards.front: Why did Joseon-dynasty elites adopt Confucianism as the central state ideology?
cards.back: They wanted to be closer to Chinese political thought

cards.front: When did Christianity arrive in Korea, and how was it first received?
cards.back: In the 1700s — as heretical and dangerous, and it was persecuted

cards.front: What is Korea's standing in Christianity in Asia today?
cards.back: The second most Christian country in Asia, and the second largest producer of Christian missionaries

cards.front: Why did Christianity appeal to the lower classes in Korea?
cards.back: Its egalitarian doctrine, against a backdrop of corruption and ineffectualness

cards.front: What helped Christianity gain traction after Japan annexed Korea?
cards.back: Support from the U.S. Army Military Government, and President Rhee Syngman, who vowed to rule South Korea as a Christian nation

cards.front: What do some scholars claim about the antiquity of Korean shamanism?
cards.back: That it goes back to prehistoric times, when Korea was ruled by shaman-kings who were both political and religious leaders

cards.front: What displaced Korean shamanism?
cards.back: Buddhism and Confucianism

cards.front: How long has shamanism been attacked by Korean elites, and with what result?
cards.back: For the last 600 years — yet it has never come close to extinction

cards.front: How is Korean shamanism regarded today?
cards.back: As superstitious and irrational

cards.front: On what axiom does North Korea ban religion?
cards.back: The communist axiom that religion is the opium of the masses

cards.front: What is known about the Buddhist temples and Christian churches in North Korea?
cards.back: Little — information is very hard to get; those familiar think what is practised illustrates state propaganda of religious freedom

cards.meaning: North Korea's unquestioned belief in the superiority of its system and the leadership of the Kim family — standing in place of religion

cards.front: How is South Korea described religiously today?
cards.back: As a multi-religious society

cards.front: Which religion is named as having made sizeable gains in South Korea?
cards.back: Islam
